query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is governed by the accumulation of dislocations at nanoscale interfaces enhanced by lattice distortion and short-range order. This accumulation localizes stress and activates interface sliding and shear banding, steering the system away from uniform bulk creep.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers with nanoscale layer thickness, exhibiting severe lattice distortions and possible short-range order.
generation.intervention: Application of a constant stress level (near but below the macroscopic yield strength) over a prolonged period (creep loading) on the multilayer samples.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at temperatures below recrystallization and with controlled strain rates, ensuring that the multilayer structure (layer thickness and interface coherence) is maintained. A systematic controlled comparison will be made using multilayer samples with deliberately varied interface bonding (e.g., by tuning deposition parameters) versus monolithic HEA samples of equivalent overall composition.
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation pile-ups at multilayer interfaces, which are enhanced by the high lattice distortion inherent to the alloy system, mediate local stress concentration and subsequent interface sliding.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained loading, dislocations nucleate and progressively accumulate at the interfaces due to the barrier imposed by adjacent layers. The resultant local stress concentration triggers interface sliding and eventually shear band formation. This sequential activation of localized deformation mechanisms leads to progressive plasticity that is distinct from homogeneous creep observed in monolithic counterparts.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a homogeneous baseline (e.g., monolithic HEA), the multilayer structure will exhibit localized regions of plastic deformation at the interfaces, observable as increased dislocation density and the initiation of shear bands specifically at these sites. Samples with stronger, more coherent interfaces (or lower lattice mismatch) will delay the onset of these localized mechanisms and show a lower overall plastic strain compared to samples with weaker interfaces.
generation.baseline: Monolithic high-entropy alloy samples with similar composition that deform more uniformly under the same sustained load.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the setting of nanoscale multilayer coatings where the layer thickness is maintained; deviations in temperature (e.g., approaching recrystallization temperatures) or extremely high strain rates that might bypass interface-mediated mechanisms are excluded.
generation.uncertainty: There is moderate uncertainty regarding the extent to which interface strength versus intrinsic lattice distortion controls the progression of plasticity. Variations in processing conditions (e.g., deposition-induced interdiffusion) may also influence the observations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoscale HEA multilayers: one set where interface bonding is intentionally strengthened (via optimized deposition parameters to reduce interfacial defects) and another set where interfaces are weakened (by promoting interdiffusion). Subject both sets, along with monolithic HEA samples, to identical constant-stress creep experiments while conducting in-situ microscopy (e.g., TEM) to monitor microstructural evolution.
measurements: Quantitative dislocation density at the interfaces
Progression and distribution of shear bands
Interface composition and structure before/after loading
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If variations in interface strength (i.e., expected differences in dislocation pile-up and initiation of interface sliding) do not yield measurable differences in localized deformation behavior compared to the monolithic baseline, or if localized interface deformation is not observed despite differences in interface properties, then the hypothesis that interface-mediated dislocation accumulation governs progressive plastic deformation would be falsified.
